what_it_does: Light-based computer chips use tiny ring-shaped optical components called microring resonators to route data as pulses of light at specific colors (wavelengths), which avoids the electrical interference that slows conventional wires. The problem is that the manufacturing process is never perfectly consistent — microscopic variations in how each ring is fabricated shift the precise color of light it responds to, causing signals to weaken or bleed into neighboring channels. This paper builds a mathematical model to predict how much signal power is lost across a chip under realistic manufacturing variation. It then jointly optimizes two design choices — the physical size of each ring and the specific wavelengths assigned to each data channel — so that the expected signal strength is maximized even when manufacturing is imperfect. By tuning both geometry and wavelength together rather than separately, the method exploits interactions between the two that single-variable tuning would miss.
